slides.text: Every integer type holds a fixed range. A `u8` holds 0 to 255, so asking it to hold 256 is an **overflow**. Going below 0 in an unsigned type is the same problem from the other side.

Rust does not agree with itself on what an overflow does. A debug build (`cargo run`) panics. A release build (`cargo run --release`) skips the check and wraps around silently, which hides the bug.

So code that can really overflow says what it wants, with a method that names the behavior.

Each integer has a family of methods, one per behavior. They share the operation name (`add`, `sub`, `mul`) and change the prefix. `x` and `y` below are placeholders. `Option` has its own course later: here it is only printed or unwrapped with `unwrap_or`.

- `wrapping_`: wraps around to the other end of the range
- `checked_`: gives back an `Option`, `None` when the result does not fit
- `saturating_`: stops at the nearest edge of the range
- `overflowing_`: gives back the wrapped result and whether it wrapped

This session covers the first three.

exercises.title: Wrap around
exercises.guide: Add past the edge of a `u8` and let it wrap.

chunks.guide: A `u8` close to its maximum of 255.
250 plus 10 is 260, which does not fit. The result wraps around and counts on from 0.

notes.text: Adds, and wraps past the maximum back to zero.

chunks.guide: Subtracting can wrap too, past 0 up to the top.

notes.text: Goes below zero and lands at the top of the range.

exercises.title: Debug or release?
exercises.guide: Run the code in a debug build and in a release build, then pick what each prints.
exercises.explanation: The second round needs 258, which does not fit a `u8`. A debug build panics there, a release build wraps to 2 and goes on to 6.

exercises.title: Check before you add
exercises.guide: Ask for the sum and get `None` when it does not fit.

chunks.guide: A `u8` close to its maximum.
250 plus 5 fits in a `u8`. 250 plus 6 does not.

notes.text: Gives Some(sum), or None when the sum does not fit.

chunks.text:
let fits = stock.checked_add(5);
    let full = stock.checked_add(6);

chunks.guide: Print both results. They are not plain numbers: each is `Some(number)` or `None`.
Take the number out, with a fallback for `None`.

notes.text: Gives the number, or 0 when there is none.

exercises.title: A sum that cannot wrap
exercises.guide: Add 10 without wrapping, then print the sum, or 0 when it does not fit.

exercises.title: Removing too many
exercises.guide: Handle an order bigger than the stock in two ways, and one that fits.

chunks.guide: An unsigned stock cannot go below 0, and an order may ask for more than it holds.
chunks.text:
let stock: u32 = 12;
    let order: u32 = 15;

chunks.guide: Refuse the order: when it does not fit, the stock stays as it was.

notes.text: Falls back to the old stock when the order is too big.

chunks.guide: Sell everything: the stock stops at zero.
A small order of 5 fits, so the refusing version removes it.

exercises.title: Pick the behavior
exercises.guide: The three lines are pseudo code, not real Rust. A health bar stops at 0, a balance refuses a bad subtraction, a hash keeps growing. Pick the prefix for each line.
exercises.code:
health  = health  - damage
balance = balance - withdrawal
hash    = hash    * 31
exercises.explanation: A bar clamps at its edge, a balance must report that it cannot go below zero, and a hash is meant to wrap and keep only the low bits.

exercises.title: Count the wraps
exercises.guide: Sum four bytes in a loop and count how many times the sum wrapped.

chunks.guide: Four bytes, a running sum and a counter for wraps.
Add each byte. The method gives the wrapped sum and a flag, split by a pattern. Count a wrap when the flag is true.

notes.text: Gives the wrapped sum and whether it wrapped.

chunks.guide: Print the checksum and the wraps: 300 wrapped to 44, and 314 to 58.

exercises.title: The edges of i32
exercises.guide: Cross both ends of an `i32`, and meet a trap of `abs`.

chunks.guide: The two edges of an `i32`, as in integers.
chunks.text:
let top = i32::MAX;
    let bottom = i32::MIN;

chunks.guide: One past the maximum wraps to the minimum.
One below the minimum wraps to the maximum.
Even `abs` can overflow: the minimum has no positive twin, so the fallback 0 is used.

notes.text: The absolute value, or None when it does not fit.

exercises.title: A health bar
exercises.guide: `left` stops at 0 when the hit is too big. `safe` is 99 in that case.

exercises.title: Why wrapping?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick what it is for.
options: Mixes numbers, capping them at the maximum
Mixes numbers with arithmetic meant to wrap
Mixes numbers, panicking if they grow too big
Mixes numbers, giving None when they overflow
exercises.explanation: A hash grows past the range on purpose and keeps only the low bits, so it needs the wrapping methods, never a panic or a clamp.

exercises.title: A counter that wraps
exercises.guide: Count up past the top of a `u8` without panicking in a debug build.

chunks.guide: A counter close to the top of a `u8`.
Count up ten times. A plain `+= 1` would panic here, so the wrapping method does the step.
The counter passed 255 and went on from 0.

slides.text: `overflowing_` gives back two values in a tuple: the wrapped result and a `bool` that says whether it wrapped. A pattern splits them into two names.

The constants you met in integers are the numbers a method reaches when it clamps or wraps. Two methods work at those edges: `overflowing_` hands back the wrapped result with a flag, and signed types have a trap of their own.
Signed types have one more trap: `abs`. The minimum has no positive twin, so `abs` can overflow like any other operation, and `checked_abs` exists for it.
